title: Understand and Integrate Security in the SDLC
objective: Study-guide review — CISSP — Domain 8: Software Development Security: Understand and Integrate Security in the SDLC.

blocks.text: The SDLC defines the structured process for developing software:

items: Conceptual Definition / Feasibility — determine if the project makes sense; examine requirements and proposed functionality; brainstorming sessions; review obvious restrictions
Requirements Gathering — define functional and non-functional requirements, including security requirements
Design — architecture and design decisions; threat modeling; security architecture review
Development / Coding — write the code following secure coding standards
Testing / Validation — verify the software meets requirements; includes security testing (SAST, DAST, penetration testing)
Deployment / Release — move to production; includes final security review, hardening, change management
Operations and Maintenance — ongoing support, patching, monitoring, incident response
Disposal / Retirement — secure decommissioning; data sanitization; archival
Security must be integrated into EVERY phase — not bolted on at the end
Requirements phase should include security requirements alongside functional requirements
Security risks should be identified as part of change management, and requirements must be documented and carried through all SDLC phases

blocks.text: A conceptual definition of the project should be developed during the feasibility phase. The team examines the software's requirements and proposed functionality, brainstorming sessions take place, and obvious restrictions are reviewed. This early phase should include a preliminary security assessment to identify potential security concerns before significant resources are committed. The key principle is "shift left" — moving security activities earlier in the SDLC rather than treating security as a final gate. Finding and fixing vulnerabilities during design or development is significantly cheaper than fixing them after deployment. Studies suggest that fixing a bug in production can cost 30-100x more than fixing it during design. Security activities by phase:

items: Requirements: Security requirements, compliance requirements, data classification
Design: Threat modeling, security architecture review, design patterns
Development: Secure coding standards, code review, unit testing
Testing: SAST, DAST, penetration testing, security regression testing
Deployment: Security hardening, configuration review, final security assessment
Operations: Monitoring, patching, incident response, vulnerability management
Disposal: Data sanitization, certificate revocation, access removal

blocks.title: Exam trap
blocks.text: ⚠️ Exam Trap: Security must be part of EVERY SDLC phase. If the exam asks when security should be considered, the answer is "from the beginning" or "throughout the entire lifecycle" — never just at the end or during testing only.

rows: Waterfall
Sequential, linear phases; each phase must complete before the next begins
Simple, rigid; no going back; poor for changing requirements
V-Model
Extension of Waterfall; each development phase has a corresponding testing phase
Testing is planned early; still sequential
Spiral
Iterative; repeats phases in spirals with increasing detail; emphasizes risk analysis
Risk-driven; good for large, complex projects
Iterative/Incremental
Software built in increments; each iteration adds functionality
More flexible than Waterfall; working software early
Prototyping
Build quick prototypes to validate requirements before full development
Reduces misunderstanding of requirements; prototype may be discarded
RAD (Rapid Application Development)
Emphasizes rapid prototyping and user feedback over rigid planning
Fast development; may sacrifice quality

blocks.text: The Waterfall model is the oldest and most straightforward — it proceeds through phases sequentially: requirements → design → implementation → testing → deployment → maintenance. Its primary weakness is inflexibility — if requirements change after the design phase, it is very difficult and expensive to go back. The Spiral model, introduced by Barry Boehm, addresses Waterfall's limitations by incorporating iterative development with explicit risk analysis. Each "spiral" includes: determine objectives, identify risks, develop and test, plan the next iteration. The emphasis on risk analysis makes it particularly suitable for security-critical projects. The key exam distinction is between sequential models (Waterfall, V-Model) and iterative models (Spiral, Agile). Sequential models are predictable but inflexible; iterative models are flexible but require more management discipline.

items: Threat modeling — identify threats during design phase; use STRIDE, DREAD, PASTA, or attack trees
Security requirements — define alongside functional requirements; include authentication, authorization, encryption, audit logging
Secure design principles — defense in depth, least privilege, fail-secure, separation of duties, secure defaults
Security testing — integrated throughout development, not just at the end
Security reviews / gates — formal review points where security is evaluated before proceeding to the next phase
Risks should be identified as part of change management, documented, and carried through all SDLC phases to address these risks appropriately and test the mitigations in place
Iterative, incremental approach with short development cycles (sprints, typically 2-4 weeks)

Scrum — framework within Agile; defines roles (Scrum Master, Product Owner, Development Team), events (Sprint, Daily Standup, Sprint Review, Sprint Retrospective), and artifacts (Product Backlog, Sprint Backlog)
Kanban — visual workflow management; continuous flow rather than fixed sprints
Emphasizes collaboration, working software, and responding to change
Security considerations: security stories/tasks in the backlog, automated security testing in CI/CD
Scales Agile practices to large enterprises
Four levels: Essential SAFe, Large Solution SAFe, Portfolio SAFe, Full SAFe
Full SAFe includes all elements of the other levels and is designed to support enterprises that build and maintain large, integrated solutions requiring hundreds of practitioners
Emphasizes pair programming, test-driven development (TDD), continuous integration
Security benefits: code review through pairing, comprehensive testing
DevOps — culture and practices that unite software development (Dev) and IT operations (Ops)
DevSecOps — integrates security into the DevOps pipeline as a first-class concern
Continuous Integration (CI) — developers frequently merge code changes; automated builds and tests run on each merge
Continuous Delivery (CD) — code is always in a deployable state; deployment can happen at any time
Continuous Deployment — every change that passes automated tests is automatically deployed to production
Infrastructure as Code (IaC) — infrastructure defined in version-controlled code files; enables automated, repeatable deployments
Security in DevSecOps: automated SAST/DAST in pipeline, security unit tests, container scanning, dependency checking, secrets management

blocks.text: DevSecOps shifts security left by embedding it directly into the CI/CD pipeline. Rather than security being a separate gate at the end of development, security testing is automated and runs with every code commit. This includes:

items: Pre-commit hooks for secrets detection
SAST scanning on every pull request
Dependency/SCA scanning for known vulnerabilities in libraries
Container image scanning before deployment
DAST scanning against staging environments
Infrastructure-as-code security scanning (e.g., Terraform security analysis)

blocks.text: The goal is to make security feedback as fast as possible — developers should know about security issues within minutes of committing code, not weeks later during a separate security review.

items: CMMI (Capability Maturity Model Integration) — framework for improving organizational processes:

rows: Initial
Processes are unpredictable, reactive, ad hoc
Managed
Processes are planned and managed at the project level
Defined
Processes are standardized across the organization
Quantitatively Managed
Processes are measured and controlled using statistics
Optimizing
Focus on continuous process improvement

items: SAMM (Software Assurance Maturity Model) — OWASP framework specifically for software security maturity
BSIMM (Building Security In Maturity Model) — descriptive model based on observed software security practices across organizations
IDEAL Model — Initiating, Diagnosing, Establishing, Acting, Learning — process improvement model

blocks.text: CMMI provides a structured framework for evaluating and improving an organization's software development maturity. The five levels represent a progression from chaotic, ad hoc processes (Level 1) to fully optimized processes with continuous improvement (Level 5). Key exam points:

items: Level 1 (Initial): No formal processes; success depends on individual effort ("heroic" developers)
Level 2 (Managed): Basic project management exists; processes are repeated for similar projects
Level 3 (Defined): Organization-wide standard processes exist and are documented
Level 4 (Quantitatively Managed): Metrics are collected and used to manage processes
Level 5 (Optimizing): Continuous improvement through quantitative feedback

blocks.title: Exam trap
blocks.text: ⚠️ Exam Trap: Know the five CMMI levels and their names. Level 1 is "Initial" (not "None" or "Incomplete"). The levels represent organizational maturity, not individual project quality.
